newsitem.title: FRANCE: UK's Cook seeks new era of closer ties with Europe.
newsitem.headline: UK's Cook seeks new era of closer ties with Europe.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook, in Paris on his maiden trip abroad, said he wanted a new era of warmer ties with Europe and agreed to work with France for a global ban on anti-personnel mines.

But he set limits on Britain's enthusiasm for European integration, saying the Labour party would not abandon British border controls after its landslide election win last week ended 18 years of Conservative rule.

"We want Britain to be one of the three leading members of the European Union (with France and Germany), working together to achieve an outcome in the interests of all our peoples," he said after meeting Foreign Minister Herve de Charette.

"It is our commitment that we will draw a line under the sterile, negative and fruitless confrontation which was the policy of the previous British government," he said. "I want to make sure that Britain has a fresh start in Europe."

De Charette and Cook, who was due to meet German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel in Bonn later on Wednesday, said they had agreed a joint effort to ban anti-personnel landmines and hoped Germany would also join in.

"We hope we will be able today to make a tripartite statement committing our three countries to work together to achieve a ban on the landmines that have caused so much suffering around the world," Cook said.

De Charette said the three countries "were interested in accelerating the process of talks in this area". He said France "attaches great importance to the quality and density of the relations between our two countries".

Cook said Britain and France would work together to try to find a joint position on reform of EU institutions in the inter-governmental conference (IGC), due to be completed by the June EU summit in Amsterdam.

"We want to go to the Amsterdam conference hoping to set the direction of the conference," he said. The Labour government has also said it will sign the Social Chapter of the Maastricht Treaty at the Amsterdam summit.
"At the same time, Britain will of course insist on the protection of its vital national interests, such as our anxiety to make sure we preserve our external border controls," he said.
EU negotiators are close to agreement on a deal to make an existing pact on border-free travel, the Schengen Agreement, part of the EU treaty, with opt-outs for Britain and Ireland.
Cook did not mention the likelihood of Britain joining a single European currency. Labour has retained the right not to join and promised to hold a referendum before any decision is taken.

Cook, who also met French opposition Socialist leader Lionel Jospin, declined to say whether he would prefer the Socialists or France's ruling centre-right coalition to win the snap parliamentary election on May 25-June 1.
He said the French Socialists were Labour's "sister party" but said: "We will work very closely with whomever the French people choose to govern them."
Politicians in France's government say the policies of the new British government are more akin to the ruling coalition's free-market approach than the more leftist recipes of the French Socialists.
"Everybody wishes to be (Prime Minister) Tony Blair at the moment," Cook said.

French European Affairs Minister Michel Barnier praised what he called the new British government's very constructive approach to the EU. "We were not expecting a revolution, but we did hope for a new climate. What we have felt so far is this new climate," he said.
He said it was a "very positive signal" that Britain had decided to be represented at ministerial level at IGC talks.
